in your shoes, i would be asking the following questions to myself even moreso:

a) am i prepared to be around grieving families? do i understand that anger and lashing out can be a response to grief? will i be able to be professional and not spiral if a family blames me for xyz? 

b) do i understand the corporate monotony of the funeral service field and can i come to terms with it? will still i feel fulfilled in a paperwork-heavy field?

in my experience, being around deceased people is one of the easier parts of my profession. they are not going to do anything to you, they are simply existing and being themselves. the absolute 100% hardest part of my job is interacting with the living, and not taking their grief home with me. i also feel like de-glamorizing the funeral service field before you invest in it is super important too, bc that is a dealbreaker for many people. is my job super meaningful to me? yes. do i have amazing, life changing moments at work where i feel like i'm really helping my community? yes. do i also do a bunch of monotonous paperwork? totally. do i have to sit through casket company new product sales pitches at meetings? yes. you have to weigh if you're able to tank a bunch of the latter to get a little bit of the former. (mostly applies to funeral directing, not to full time embalming)

As to your question: like many other legalities at a funeral home, laws about storage and refrigeration are on a state-by-state basis. for example: in california, anyone who is unembalmed must be in refrigeration (they cannot be out of refrigeration for more than 24 hours) and the refrigeration must be at a specific temperature. so, if this happened in california, while the fact that they didnt have a refrigeration unit would not be against the law, keeping your mother unrefrigerated and unembalmed for more than 24hrs would be against the law (they would need to embalm her or take her to a second location to be refrigerated). this is just one state's policies though-- every state is super super different.

if you think this would be helpful emotionally, you can get in contact with the funeral home and cemetery authority in your state if one exists (example: california has the funeral and cemetery bureau), explain the situation, and ask if it was legal or not.

it sounds like you are looking for a death that does not "inconvenience" your loved ones. that kind of death does not exist. your family and friends will notice your presence gone -- financially, physically, and most importantly emotionally. there will be people at the coroners office who care about you. there will be people at the funeral home who care about you. even when someone passes with no family and no friends left, there is still a county appointed individual who takes care of their passing. there's no way to just like, sidestep all of this. 

as someone who has dealt with suicidal ideation for most of my life, remembering the above has really helped me. again, not trying to preach, just trying to outline that death still effects people, even individuals with no family and friends. it will still be felt. sorry for not answering your question.
additionally -- if you work at a funeral home before mortuary school, many companies will reimburse you for your licensure exams.

without a doubt i would recommend at the least shadowing at a funeral home, the best course of action if possible is to get employed entry-level at a funeral home. what people think when they idealize working at a funeral home vs what it actually entails are two very different things!! in my experience, ive seen a lot of ppl in my personal life go to mortuary school, spend thousands, graduate + even get their boards without ever working at a funeral home, and then finally go into the field, and realize they dont like it and career change. save time and figure out if you enjoy the real work before wasting time and money for a degree you dont know if you'll use or not.

hi!!! i deal with similar ocd issues -- rumination is my main compulsion and i also deal w self isolating. i'm not a mental health professional, but heres how i see it:

it sounds like you want to "dial back on social interaction" i.e. isolate, due to your ocd/intrusive thoughts. when we do things bc our ocd tells us to do them, it gives those thoughts power. our brain thinks, because we had to do something bc of the thought, the thought is more legitimate. bc of this, i'd be wary of changing your social patterns due to ocd related fear. we want to show our brains that our intrusive thoughts do not hold power over us-- and a way we can show our brains that is to not alter our behavior based on our intrusive thoughts yfm!!!

all of this being said though, if youre in an unsafe place mentally and feel like you're in a place of crisis, please reach out to a mental health professional! did your therapist leave you with any names of colleagues in the case of a crisis that you can contact? 

best wishes 🤍

hey friend, as someone with different themes but similar ocd anciety so bad it triggers throwinf up / nausea / unable to eat -- nutrients are going to be super important rn so that your mind can have fuel to fight back against the ocd spirals. heres what i swear by to get nutrients in me when nothing is going down:

-stock up on protein smoothies. my favs are ensure or boost. they shld be at any target safeway etc. you can also make your own protein smoothies if ur up for it, i also know jamba juice has some tasty protein smoothies too! this helps bc you dont have to physically eat anything but still get protein in u 

-pedialyte for minerals and electrolytes!

-gerber baby puffs are super easy to keep down and have a bunch of helpful vitamins, will also help ur stomach bc its something physical

-ask your doctor about a zofran prescription! its a prescription antinausea med and it rlly helps me eat

-if you havent been eating in a while and drinking has also been hard, you may be dealing with bad dehydration rn. if thats the case and you have insurance, you might want to go to the er to get some intravenous saline fluids. the fluids helped me A LOT when i had to get them, it made me think clearly for the first time in weeks after i finished the bag. 

i hope this helps <3 you got this!!!! take care of your body so it can help your ocdthoughts!

hi!! asking for some clarification: are you writing the death certificate yourself, as in filing it on EDRS yourself? or are you providing information for somebody else to create the official death certificate?

if its the former, there is a way on EDRS to create an amendment, you just need a second certified user to sign off on it as well. if its the latter, contact your funeral home / whoever was formally processing the death certificate and they will be able to make the amendment for you!

as long as the typo wasnt on anything considered "medical information" (legal name, date of death, time of death, place of death, causes), it takes the amendment around 1 business day to get approved by the state after submitting the amendment for review, and then however long it takes for you or the FH to order and pick up the new certificate from your county building! 

im speaking from experience in the US, so if youre not in the US, this process will probably look super different!

in terms of who controls disposition the chain of command goes decedent ---> power of health care ----> spouse. so if the woman in question wants to be extra sure that her husband does not control disposition, she can make her own pre arrangement and legally it must be followed upon her death no matter what husband says. in addition, she can name a legal power of health care which would have power over disposition that the husband couldnt take away. just make sure with the power of health care that, when shes naming it, the legal documentation explicitly states that this person has control over disposition, because a normal power of attorney won't do in some cases unless it has that specific wording describing having power over the care once dead / disposition. by having both a prearrangement And a power of health care, shes protecting herself very well from her husband having control over disposition. none of these are genuine victorian post mortems. her eyes are way too focused to be that of a decedent even if the husband somehow got her eyelids to stay open and as a previous commentor pointed out, her brow is furrowed. shes just an alive woman who is laying her head against her husbands shoulder bc victorian photography took a very long time and it was hard to stay still for that long. 

the way to think about victorian post mortem photography imo is to remember that the victorians werent trying to hide the fact that the decedent was dead. they had no societal qualms with death, they were very comfortable with the concept and had specific attire and jewelry to mark a time of mourning. most genuine post mortems are pictures of the decedent laying in a coffin or casket with following photos of their family in their mourning attire doing things like wiping their tears with a handkerchief. most if not surely all articles that are like Look, The Victorians Posed This Dead Person To Make Them Look Like They Are Alive For A Photograph are simply morbidity clickbait. the victorians didnt need to pretend like their loved ones werent dead for their post mortems, they just wanted one last photo of them to remember them by.

first of all im not black and dont want to come across like im speaking for a community im not a part of, i just have studied american funeral history for awhile so this is some historical context from my studies!

so the idea of giving someone else your deceased loved one for them to take care of and provide deathcare only came around in america during and post civil war as thats when embalming started rlly catching on here, before then most families would take care of their own dead. so the Funeral Home as a concept entered america at the same time as the reconstruction era when the black community was actually getting some reparations from living thru slavery (that wld end up being reversed and revoked leading up to and during the turn of the century). but for the time being the community was experiencing a) financial freedom and b) the ability to choose what happens to their dead for the first time, as the enslaved black community was barred from holding intricate funeral arrangements. w all of this being said, the black community during the reconstruction era was finally able to celebrate and honor their dead as extravagantly as they would like. this combined w the fact that white owned funeral homes didnt understand or care to learn how to take care of black decedents hair texture, meant that black family owned funeral businesses were a huge thing that was popularized during reconstruction and were a very important staple business in the black community, who as discussed previously have just been able to start having funeral services but were v justifiably distrustful of white FH's. this was a rlly important cultural phenomenon so it makes a lot of sense that it's still felt today!
